title: Four months back with Zig and community meetups
excerpt: After four months away, the author revisits Zig, builds snurl, and attends a local Zig Day, noting pros, cons, and community vibes.
body:
Four months after a long break, the author returned to Zig and put together snurl, a tiny library that talks to the “smallnet” protocols, Gemini, Finger, Gopher, Spartan, and friends. The goal was to give those services a curl-like command line tool, with testing and fuzzing kept to a modest scale and the TigerStyle guidelines followed where they made sense.

During that period the author also built a TUI typer-racer and an n-body simulator that uses raylib for graphics. Those side projects show that Zig can handle both quick prototypes and more demanding workloads, as long as the tooling gaps are understood.

The following sections walk through the most notable experiences: the first Zig codebase, the missing fuzzing support, the community boost from Zig Days, and the explicit allocator model that sets Zig apart from languages like Rust and Odin. By the end, you’ll know which trade-offs to expect when picking Zig for a low-level project.

## First Zig codebase: the snurl library  

Snurl became the author’s re-entry point into Zig. It wraps network calls for the smallnet protocols and exposes a thin, composable API. Parsing URLs, opening sockets, and handling TLS all fell into place with relatively little boilerplate, thanks to Zig’s standard library.  

Early in development a snag appeared: the `main.zig` file generated by `zig init` mentions a fuzzer, but the feature was not yet functional. The author discovered that the fuzzer demo does not actually run, a fact that matches the broader state of Zig’s tooling as described in the source article.  

Despite the missing fuzzing, the core of snurl shipped quickly, and the author was able to start experimenting with alternative TLS back-ends later in the same month.

## Fuzzing support is still a work in progress  

The generated `main.zig` file can give a false impression that fuzz testing is ready out of the box. In reality, the fuzzer demo ships with the language but does not execute, a gap the community is aware of. The source notes that this is “not surprising, considering Zig’s status,” yet the disappointment is real when a project’s testing plan relies on fuzzing.  

Because the feature is incomplete, the author had to postpone the fuzzing stage for snurl and focus on manual tests instead. The article hopes the built-in fuzzing will be fixed soon, especially after a brief conversation with Andrew Kelley at a local meetup.

## Zig Days turn meetups into pair-programming sessions  

Zig Day Seattle was announced on Lobsters on August 20 and quickly filled the Bellevue library, prompting a move to the larger Bothell library. Andrew Kelley, Zig’s creator, attended, and the author joined a friend, Evin Yulo, to work on snurl together.  

During the event Evin started integrating Zig’s standard-library TLS implementation as an alternative backend, demonstrating how the meetup format encourages hands-on collaboration. The author also chatted with several other programmers, exchanging ideas that may influence future projects.  

Ryan Hendrickson later published a detailed recap of the day, confirming the community-driven vibe described in the source. The author plans to attend future Zig Days in Seattle and possibly Portland, citing the value of face-to-face interaction for a language that still relies heavily on community support.

## Explicit allocator handling makes memory intent clear  

Zig requires every function that allocates memory to receive an explicit allocator parameter. Unlike languages that hide allocation behind a global or implicit context, Zig forces the caller to state the allocation strategy at the call site.  

This design lets developers swap an arena allocator for short-lived work, a general-purpose allocator for larger structures, or a `FixedBufferAllocator` when a fixed-size buffer suffices. The author prefers this explicitness over Odin’s implicit context system because it reduces the chance of accidentally using the wrong allocator and makes memory-usage intent obvious in the code.  

The source mentions that this requirement “frustrates some people,” but also highlights the benefit of being able to change allocators for different parts of a program without surprising side effects.

## The takeaway  

Zig’s explicit allocator model and its tight-knit community provide a solid foundation for low-level projects, even though built-in fuzzing remains unfinished. Attending a Zig Day can accelerate development on libraries like snurl and open doors to collaboration that are hard to find online. Understanding the current tooling gaps, and planning around them, helps turn Zig’s strengths into reliable, production-ready code.
